extract:
The Verve formed in Wigan, a former mill town in Greater Manchester, England, in 1990. They were active in three distinct phases: 1990 to 1995, 1997 to 1999, and a brief reunion from 2007 to 2009. The classic lineup was singer Richard Ashcroft, guitarist Nick McCabe, bassist Simon Jones and drummer Peter Salisbury, most of whom had met as students at Winstanley College. They emerged in the post-Madchester north of England but leaned less toward baggy dance rhythms than toward psychedelic, effects-drenched guitar rock. McCabe's sprawling, textural playing set the template, and Ashcroft's charismatic, mystic frontman persona earned him the nickname "Mad Richard."

Originally called simply Verve, the band signed to Hut Records, a Virgin offshoot, in 1991. They released the singles "All in the Mind," "She's a Superstar" and "Gravity Grave," followed by The Verve EP in 1992. Their debut album, A Storm in Heaven (1993), was produced by John Leckie. It was a hazy, improvisational record closer to shoegaze and space rock than to the emerging Britpop sound, and "Blue" and "Slide Away" were among its singles. A legal challenge from the American jazz label Verve Records forced them to add "The" to their name in 1994. That same year they played Lollapalooza, a tour marked by excess: Salisbury was arrested after a hotel-room incident, and Ashcroft was hospitalised with dehydration.

A Northern Soul (1995), produced by Owen Morris, who was then working with Oasis, was tighter and more song-focused. It yielded "This Is Music," "On Your Own" and the string-laden "History." The band split around the release of "History." Their friendship with Oasis was well known, and Noel Gallagher dedicated "Cast No Shadow" to Ashcroft. Within months Ashcroft reconvened the group, adding guitarist and keyboardist Simon Tong, and McCabe soon returned.

The resulting album, Urban Hymns (1997), co-produced with Youth and Chris Potter, made them one of Britain's biggest bands. "Bitter Sweet Symphony" was built on a sample of the Andrew Oldham Orchestra's orchestral version of the Rolling Stones' "The Last Time." It became a worldwide hit, but a dispute with ABKCO and Allen Klein transferred the song's writing credit and royalties to Jagger and Richards. In 2019 the two Stones relinquished their share to Ashcroft. "The Drugs Don't Work" gave the band their first UK number one, and "Lucky Man" and "Sonnet" followed as singles. Urban Hymns won Best British Album at the 1998 Brit Awards, and "Bitter Sweet Symphony" received a Grammy nomination. Tensions resurfaced, however. McCabe left during the 1998 touring cycle, and the band dissolved in 1999.

Ashcroft launched a solo career with Alone with Everybody (2000), while Tong later worked with Blur's Damon Albarn in Gorillaz and The Good, the Bad & the Queen. The original four reunited in 2007, headlined Glastonbury in 2008, and released Forth that year, led by the single "Love Is Noise." The reunion proved short-lived, and the band split again in 2009.

The Verve's legacy rests on a striking arc, from cult psychedelic outfit to stadium-scale balladeers. "Bitter Sweet Symphony" remains one of the defining songs of late-1990s British rock, endlessly licensed and frequently cited in debates about sampling and copyright. Their early records are also remembered as a bridge between shoegaze and Britpop. Ashcroft continues to record and tour as a solo artist, regularly performing Verve material.
title: The Verve
